results.title: A Multi-match Approach to the Author Uncertainty Problem
results.content: In this study we build on the author identifier approach by considering commonalities in fielded data between authors containing the same surname and first initial of their first name. The approach we advance in this study is based on commonalities among fielded data in search results. We find email addresses similarly adequate—e.g., if two author names which share the same surname and same first initial have an email address in common, we conclude these authors are the same person. Commonalities among author data other than unique identifiers and email addresses is less conclusive for name consolidation purposes. Our approach makes use of automation as well as manual inspection, relying initially on author identifiers, then commonalities among fielded data other than author identifiers, and finally manual verification. It then prompts the user to select a WOS field on which to consolidate author names. After this the user is prompted to point to the name of the authors field, and finally asked to identify a specific author name (referred to by the script as the primary author) within this field whom the user knows to be a true positive (a suggested approach is to point to an author name associated with one of the records that has the author’s ORCID iD or email address attached to it). The script proceeds to identify and combine all author names sharing the primary author’s surname and first initial of his or her first name who share commonalities in the WOS field on which the user was prompted to consolidate author names. The procedure we advance has the ability to save a significant amount of time and effort for individuals engaged in name disambiguation research, especially when the name under consideration is a more common family name. The procedure we advance is intended to be applied across numerous fields in a dataset of interest (e.g. emails, coauthors, affiliations, etc.), resulting in multiple rounds of reduction. Results indicate that effective match fields include author identifiers, emails, source titles, co-authors and ISSNs. While the script we present is not likely to result in a dataset consisting solely of true positives (at least for more common surnames), it does significantly reduce manual effort on the user’s part.

results.title: (PDF) Effective self-training author name disambiguation in scholarly digital libraries
results.content: Supervised methods that exploit training examples in order to distinguish ambiguous author names are among the most effective solutions for the problem, but they require skilled human annotators in a laborious and continuous process of manually labeling citations in order to provide enough training examples. In this paper, we propose a novel two-step disambiguation method, SAND (Self-training Associative Name Disambiguator), that deals with these two issues. The first step eliminates the need of any manual labeling effort by automatically acquiring examples using a clustering method that groups citation records based on the similarity among coauthor names. The second step uses a supervised disambiguation method that is able to detect unseen authors not included in any of the given training examples. Experiments conducted with standard public collections, using the minimum set of attributes present in a citation (i.e., author names, work title and publication venue), demonstrated that our proposed method outperforms representative unsupervised disambiguation methods that exploit similarities between citation records and is as effective as, and in some cases superior to, supervised ones, without manually labeling any training example. results.title: ORCID‑linked labeled data for evaluating author name disambiguation at scale | by Eleventh Hour Enthusiast | Medium
results.content: # ORCID‑linked labeled data for evaluating author name disambiguation at scale. In their 2021 study, Kim and Owen-Smith investigate how ORCID — a widely used open researcher profile system — can serve as a reliable authority source for evaluating large-scale author name disambiguation methods. Their research focuses on using ORCID-linked labeled data to assess the performance of Author-ity2009, a major disambiguation system used for MEDLINE. This blog post reviews the study’s findings, focusing on the use of ORCID-linked data to compare labeling methods, its effectiveness in representing diverse author populations, and the key benefits and challenges of large-scale author name disambiguation. ORCID offers distinct advantages as a labeling source for author name disambiguation due to its extensive and structured researcher profiles. Unlike other authority sources — such as NIH-funded researcher data or highly cited researcher lists — ORCID is not limited to specific disciplines, regions, or only high-profile academics. The linkage process involved matching both paper titles and author names from MEDLINE records with corresponding data in ORCID profiles. The study also used affiliation data from ORCID profiles to strengthen the linkage process, using institutional ties as an additional verification layer when matching authors. As more researchers create ORCID profiles and expand their information, this dataset can grow dynamically, making it a continuously evolving resource for disambiguation assessments. ORCID profiles rely on voluntary registration and self-updating by researchers, leading to varying levels of completeness. Despite these gaps, the study concluded that ORCID remains one of the most effective large-scale labeling sources available, especially when combined with other bibliometric data. The study conducted a detailed comparison of ORCID-linked labeled data (AUT-ORC) with two other common labeling methods: NIH-funded Principal Investigator data (AUT-NIH) and self-citation-based labeling (AUT-SCT). ORCID-linked labeled data offers a powerful and scalable solution for evaluating author name disambiguation systems, providing broader and more inclusive coverage than traditional labeling methods. While some limitations remain — such as varying profile completeness and a slight bias toward early and mid-career researchers — ORCID-linked data significantly enhances the fairness and depth of disambiguation evaluations.
